extracted.intended_audience: medical students, clinicians, and laboratory technicians performing chemical and microscopic urinalysis
extracted.subtask_description: Practical laboratory methods and diagnostic criteria for detecting and characterizing abnormal constituents of urine (acetone, fats, blood, hemoglobin, pus, bile, indican, iodides/bromides, drugs, phenolics, etc.) using simple wet-chemistry, distillation, extraction and microscopy techniques. The page gives step-by-step reagents, expected colour reactions, sample volumes, caveats and alternative procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACÉTONE DANS l’URINE (Chautard reaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect acetone by adding a few drops of the reagent (fuchsine-based) to ~10–20 cc urine; presence of acetone causes recoloring in pink due to reappearance of fuchsine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reaction is often unreliable: low acetone concentration may fail to react and false positives (reappearance of fuchsine without acetone) can occur. Prefer to distill urine and test the distillate (see Lieben/iodoform method). Volumes: start with ~100–150 cc urine and collect first 15–20 cc of distillate (acetone boils ~56°C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distillation + production of iodoform (Lieben) for acetone
rubrics_metrics.description: After collecting the acetone-rich distillate, add iodine dissolved in potassium iodide and a little caustic potash; a precipitate of iodoform will form proportional to acetone present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iodoform is characterized by its odour and crystalline form; to obtain crystals, agitate the liquid containing iodoform with ether — ether evaporates leaving crystalline iodoform. This method is recommended over the direct Chautard reagent on whole urine because of higher reliability and concentration by distillation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matières grasses (fat detection) in urine
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize fats by: 1) a glued paper strip immersed in urine that remains stained after drying; 2) shaking a quantity of urine with ether which clears the liquid as ether extracts fats; 3) decanting and evaporating ether leaves a residue testable on paper; 4) microscopic examination to recognize fat globules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If apparent opacity is due to pus globules, microscopy will reveal pus cells and ether treatment will not clarify the liquid. Use the combination of paper staining, ether extraction, and microscopy to confirm fat presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: SANG (blood) in urine — sediment and heat/acid tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Urines containing blood vary from pale pink to dark brown, are turbid and usually albuminous. Routine check: let urine stand, examine sediment microscopically for abundant erythrocytes; filter, acidify with acetic acid and boil — an albuminous coagulum forms but will be brown if blood degradation products present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heller-style chemical characterization: boil a few cc of urine made strongly alkaline (add caustic soda) — phosphates precipitate and carry blood pigment as red-brown flocculi while the supernatant becomes bottle-green. Use microscopy plus this test to confirm blood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hémoglobinurie (hemoglobinuria) — spectroscopic identification
rubrics_metrics.description: When urine is red but contains no intact erythrocytes, hemoglobin (oxyhemoglobin) may be present in solution. Using a pocket spectroscope with a tube of filtered urine, oxyhemoglobin produces two adjacent dark absorption bands: one fine in the yellow, another slightly wider near the yellow–green boundary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To confirm the bands are due to oxyhemoglobin, reduce (deoxygenate) by adding 1–2 drops of ammonium sulfide; on re-examination the two bands should be replaced by a single broader band shifted toward the red (characteristic of deoxyhemoglobin/hemoglobin). Note other pigments (urobilin, bile pigments) can give bands in different spectral positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hémoglobinurie — alkaline boiling (alternative chemical test)
rubrics_metrics.description: If spectroscope unavailable, make urine alkaline and boil: hemoglobin is transformed to hematin, precipitating as red-brown flocculi with greenish reflections on reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This boiling-alkali test is a practical alternative though less specific than spectroscopic confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pus in urine — microscopic identification of leukocytes
rubrics_metrics.description: Purulent urine is cloudy, grayish; after settling, a gray sediment examined microscopically reveals leucocytes (rounded pale vesicles often larger than erythrocytes and with one or several nuclei). Addition of a drop of dilute acetic acid to the preparation makes nuclei more apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pus-containing urine is always albuminous; filtering the urine leaves leukocytes on the filter and albumin in the filtrate. The albumin due solely to pus is usually small — a notably large albumin amount suggests additional sources. Leukocytes are preserved well if urine is acidic and not putrid; if alkaline, they swell and disintegrate rapidly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pus characterization without microscope — alkali-induced filant mass
rubrics_metrics.description: When leukocytes have started to alter or no microscope is available: acidify urine with acetic acid, allow deposit, decant supernatant, add excess ammonia or caustic soda to the deposit and agitate vigorously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mixture rapidly becomes a filant mass like egg white and may become gelatinous if leucocyte proportion is large; alkalies convert pus globules into a muco-gelatinous mass. This property is used to characterize pus in difficult samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bile (bilirubin/pigments) in urine — appearance and Gmelin reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Bilious urines are yellow, brown or green and usually produce yellowish foam; filtered urine leaves a yellow-green stain on paper. The Gmelin reaction: place slightly nitrous nitric acid in a conical glass and gently layer urine along the wall; at the acid–urine interface oxidized bile pigments produce a ring that first appears green then may change to blue, violet, red and finally yellow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appearance of the green coloration is essential and characteristic for bile pigments; other colour bands (blue/red) can be produced by other urine components (e.g., indican). Use layered addition to minimize mixing and observe the sequence of colours at the interface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urines médicamenteuses (drug-coloured urines) — rhubarb, senna, santonin etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Urines after ingestion of rhubarb, senna or chrysophanic-containing substances may be yellow, yellow-red or yellow-green and can be confused with icteric or blood-tinged urine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nitric acid partially decolorizes these drug-coloured urines whereas it darkens bilious and sanguineous urines. Addition of an alkali (sodium hydroxide or ammonia) turns them red and they revert to original tint with acids. Santonin behaves similarly to rhubarb with these reagents — use these reactions to distinguish medicinal colouration.

rubrics_metrics.name: INDICAN in urine — chloroform extraction with HCl and hypochlorite (blue chloroform)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mix equal volumes of urine and hydrochloric acid in a test tube, add 2–3 cc chloroform, then add dilute sodium hypochlorite dropwise while inverting the tube and mixing after each addition. The chloroform gradually colors blue if indican is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A slight excess of hypochlorite has little effect, but a large excess will oxidize indigo to a yellow derivative (isatine) preventing blue coloration. If urine contains albumin, remove it beforehand (albumin interferes). This is a standard sensitive test for indican.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urines noires / darkening on exposure (melanuria and phenols)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some urines may appear brown/black or darken on exposure to air (e.g., in melanotic cancer, after phenol derivatives such as phenol or creosote exposures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darkening often develops on contact with air (oxidation). Note timing relative to exposure and disease history to interpret this observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kyestéine (iridescent pellicle) — composition and nonspecificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some urines develop a thin iridescent whitish pellicle composed of ammonio-magnesian phosphate crystals, fat globules, vibrions, and organic debris; historically associated with pregnancy (kystéine) but nonspecific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed especially in pregnant women but also in men; its presence has no precise diagnostic significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iodures / Iode dans l’urine — ferric perchloride volatilization (starch paper)
rubrics_metrics.description: Into ~10 cc urine add 8–10 drops of ferric perchloride (perchlorure de fer), cover tube mouth with starch paper, heat gently (without boiling). Iodine liberated volatilizes and forms the characteristic dark blue–violet starch–iodide colour on the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ferric perchloride oxidizes iodide to iodine which vaporizes; the starch-iodine colour on the paper is diagnostic. Ensure gentle heating and a starch-containing paper or wetted paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iodides — nitrous nitric acid + chloroform extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Add nitrous (‘lightly nitrous’) nitric acid to urine in a tube, agitate and add 1–2 cc chloroform; mix by inverting so chloroform passes through the urine. The chloroform layer at bottom becomes violet if iodine is present (iodine dissolves in chloroform).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If chloroform absent, ether will appear yellow-brown; benzine or carbon disulfide give pink-red tones. Use this as an extraction-based detection. Observe colors of organic solvent layer carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitive iodide detection — interface paper/azymes bread method and hypochlorite alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: In a footed glass pour nitrous nitric acid then gently layer urine; plunge a strip of glued paper (or fragment of azymes bread) to the bottom and a blue–violet streak at the interface indicates iodide (iodide liberated forms starch–iodide). Alternatively acidify with HCl and add Labarraque’s solution (sodium hypochlorite) dropwise to produce chlorine which liberates iodine for detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add hypochlorite slowly — an excess of chlorine will rebind iodine into a colourless combination and prevent detection. If nitrous nitric acid is not sufficiently nitrous, prepare it by adding double its volume of concentrated sulfuric acid beforehand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low-iodide detection — concentration by evaporation, calcination and extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: If iodide is present only in trace amounts or sample taken long after ingestion, evaporate large urine volumes (200–400 cc) with a little caustic potash to dryness, calcine the residue to destroy organics, exhaust residue with hot water, filter and neutralize with nitric acid; then repeat iodide tests on this concentrate (preferably chloroform extraction methods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preconcentration step increases sensitivity to detect small iodide doses (0.50–0.60 centigrammes detectable within ~12–15 hours after ingestion). Careful neutralization and avoidance of over-oxidation are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bromures in urine — concentration then chloroform extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Bromides require prior concentration (evaporation with potash, calcination, aqueous extraction, neutralization) similar to iodides; in the resulting aqueous solution add nitrous nitric acid and agitate with chloroform: the organic layer becomes orange or brown depending on bromine amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct methods 1° and 3° for iodides are not applicable to bromides. Ether will take the same tint as chloroform when bromine present. Large ingestion (5–6 g) may be needed to detect bromide directly in urine without concentration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acide salicylique / salicylates detection (ferric perchloride)
rubrics_metrics.description: Add perchloride of iron dropwise to urine; the first drops precipitate phosphates as white precipitate. After phosphates settle, further addition gives an intense violet coloration due to formation of ferric salicylate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For small quantities, filter after phosphates precipitate — the filtrate will show the characteristic violet; accentuate by adding 1–2 more drops of reagent. Doses of ~0.20–0.30 centigr. are detectable after 12–15 hours post-ingestion. For very small amounts, perform ether extraction after acidifying with HCl and test the ether extract on ferric perchloride solution (violet appearance at interface).

rubrics_metrics.name: Salol / Betol — infer via salicylic acid detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Salol (phenyl salicylate) and Betol (naphthyl salicylate) are metabolized and found in urine as salicylic acid plus phenol or naphthol derivatives; detection of salicylic acid suffices to confirm passage of parent compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the salicylic acid ferric perchloride test (or extraction) rather than attempting delicate identification of other metabolites in routine clinical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naphtol detection (Desesquelle reaction) — chloroform extraction + caustic pellet colouration
rubrics_metrics.description: Place 3–4 cc chloroform in a large test tube, fill with urine, invert 13–20 times to extract naphthol; repeat extraction with fresh urine 2–3 more times using the same chloroform to concentrate. After chloroform settles, decant urine and drop a pellet of caustic potash into the chloroform layer (it sinks to the bottom). If naphthol a is present, blue-indigo spots form on the potash; if naphthol p, blue-green spots appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A slight elevation of temperature favours the reaction. Repeat extractions increase sensitivity. This method relies on color changes on the potash pellet in the chloroform phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analgésine (antipyrine) detection — ferric perchloride reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Add perchloride of iron dropwise until no more precipitate from phosphates appears, then filter; the clear filtrate will have a blood-red colour if appreciable antipyrine is present; intensify colour with 2–3 additional drops of reagent if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reaction is not absolutely specific but is useful in typical clinical conditions and dosage ranges. Use same phosphate-precipitation filtering approach as for salicylates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Créosote and Gaïacol detection — distillation-based phenolic detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Because creosote and guaiacol derivatives are excreted as sulfur-conjugates and are volatile/phenolic, perform a small distillation: mix ~30–40 cc urine with 3–4 cc concentrated sulfuric acid, boil and collect the first 3–4 cc of distillate (phenolic constituents pass early).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This early distillate can then be subjected to phenolic-detection reactions (not fully detailed in this chunk). Distillation can be easily performed without complicated apparatus; collect minimal distillate fractions to concentrate volatile phenolics.
